alt: Six cards name the jobs evidence can do, each with the lesson’s example: illustrate (the full bus shelter), clarify (compound interest as a snowball), set a mood (the high street’s hush), exemplify (the Corner Café), associate (closing a school or church) and amplify (not one shop but twelve).
caption: Illustrate, clarify, set a mood, exemplify, associate, amplify: name the job in context.

after: ## Strategy: match the evidence to the argument, the audience and the purpose
alt: Four audiences matched to evidence: a sceptical budget committee gets a costed comparison, neighbours at a meeting get a named local resident’s story, specialist readers get a controlled study and a named authority, and young readers get a vivid analogy. The writer weighs the claim, the audience, credibility and the purpose.
caption: The same claim calls for different evidence for different audiences and purposes.

alt: A named study by a university transport department is set against “I read somewhere that...”. Three questions test any source: is it qualified to speak on this question, independent of those who would gain, and current?
caption: Choose reliable, relevant, recent sources and explain them where needed.

alt: A pool of evidence holds items that support the claim and items that cut the other way. Cherry-picking shows only the supporting items and can mislead; fair selection acknowledges the counter-evidence and explains why it does not change the conclusion, which builds credibility.
caption: Fairness about inconvenient evidence makes a writer more credible, not less.

alt: Lincoln’s analogy, “A house divided against itself cannot stand”, comes before his explicit claim that the government cannot endure half slave and half free. The analogy clarifies an abstract problem, associates the claim with the Gospels, and amplifies the stakes with “cannot stand”.
caption: A familiar image does several jobs and prepares the audience for the claim.

after: ## Worked example 1: choosing evidence for an audience and purpose
alt: For governors who value careful spending, the taxi cost comparison and the usage table are the main proof. A parent’s story works as an illustration placed after the figures, and a photograph of pupils laughing contributes little because it says nothing about need or cost.
caption: Lead with the evidence the audience needs; place the rest where it can still help.

after: ## Worked example 2: explaining what evidence does
alt: The reading-room sentence sits in the centre with four jobs around it: it exemplifies who the library serves, illustrates and sets a mood through “within sight of the radiator”, appeals to care and community, and supports the claim that the cuts hurt every part of the town.
caption: A strong answer names several jobs and links each to the claim and audience.
